newsitem.title: USA: LME explores ways to report large positions.
newsitem.headline: LME explores ways to report large positions.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange will look to a system used by U.S. regulators in developing a method of reporting large trading positions, LME chief executive David King said Friday.
"We are looking at the CFTC's (Commodity Futures Trading Commission) large trader reporting mechanism," King said at the Futures Industry Association conference here.

"We will develop a hybrid of the system more suited to our markets and will place in the public domain details of significant long and short positions in the nearby without naming the companies," he said at a panel discussion.
The reporting system will be part of the LME's response to a review of the exchange by Britain's Securities and Investments Board in the wake of the Sumitomo Corp copper crisis.
Sumitomo said last June it had lost $1.8 billion, later revised to $2.6 billion, in unauthorized copper trades carried out over 10 years primarily by its chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka.

"With regard to warehouse stocks, we will also publish the fact that certain market participants may have a percentage in tonne terms, value or volume terms of the stocks," King said. "Again, we won't name the parties, but the public will be better informed of the fact there are large participants in the market."
King said the LME also planned to include volumes, values, and highs and lows on its futures contracts and open interest on its options contracts.
He said the LME would increase its executive and restructure the way it operates.

"Governance is being addressed, transparency is being addressed, and we're looking very closely at the operations of our warehouse activities and we are also enhancing our information sharing activities," he said.
He said the LME was discussing with the Securities and Futures Authority and the London Clearing House ways of sharing information more easily and securely.

"We are exploring mechanisms where we can share information directly with NYMEX (New York Mercantile Exchange) vis-a-vis the copper markets or by regulatory channels," he added. "In principle we are very supportive of the need to share data. The Sumitomo situation was the catalyst to acclerate that."
The LME holds an extraordinary general meeting on Monday to increase its board membership to 18 from 16, four of whom will be independent directors.
